material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

# Partition study notebook

## Prior hypotheses (before physical experiments)

**H1 [tentative].** At fixed phase volumes and adequate mixing/settling, the target organic fraction should follow a finite partition relation and increase with the organic-volume fraction; material pairing changes the effective distribution ratio. The dossier suggests S2 and X0 may often favor target transfer, but pair interactions are undisclosed, so this is only a marginal prior.

**H2 [tentative].** Mixing should approach a plateau: insufficient duration/speed may reduce apparent equilibration, while beyond adequate mixing further intensity should have little effect. A paired low/high mixing comparison will test this.

**Design decision.** Use all 12 batches and one pre-separation HPLC per batch. A factorial-like material screen under common volumes/mixing will separate pair effects from volume/mixing tests. HPLC must be taken before phase removal; final assay will follow explicit termination for every batch. Numerical differences will be interpreted against instrument noise and repeatability rather than assumed exact.

# Partition study notebook

## H1 — material pairing [supported within screened conditions]
At 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L added aqueous liquid, 0.020 L extractant, 0.020 mol reagent, 120 s at 500 rpm and 120 s settling, material identity changes target partition. Pre-separation HPLC organic fractions were 0.216, 0.325, 0.387 for S0/S1/S3 with X0 (events runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0037), versus 0.269 for S2/X0 (runner-operation-0007). With S2, X1/X2/X3 gave 0.315/0.267/0.371 (runner-operation-0047, -0057, -0067). Several gaps exceed the stated 0.015 HPLC standard deviation, but each nonbaseline pair has only one batch.

The marginal dossier did not predict this ordering: S3/X0 and S2/X3 were numerically strongest in this limited screen, so solvent–extractant interaction or misaligned marginal rankings remain plausible. Equal anonymous indices have no meaning.

## H2 — phase-volume relation [tentative]
Observed HPLC phase ratios varied from 0.169 to 0.219 under nominally common added volumes, a range larger than a single stated 0.018 standard deviation. Material-dependent phase behavior, sampling/noise, or imperfect physical replication may contribute. Planned low/high extractant-volume tests will directly vary the organic fraction; conclusions should use measured phase ratio rather than added aqueous volume alone.

## H3 — mixing plateau [prediction recorded before tests]
For S2/X0 at baseline volumes, a very weak mix (5 s, 100 rpm) is predicted to give less organic transfer than an intense mix (600 s, 1000 rpm). If they agree within measurement uncertainty and baseline repeatability, mixing will be treated as already saturated or unresolved over this range.

## Phase retention
Organic-retained final assays broadly reproduce the pre-separation organic inventory (events runner-operation-0010 through -0070), supporting the operational interpretation that separation removes the other phase rather than switching a sampling label. A planned aqueous-retention batch will test the complementary inventory. Final-assay residual signal in the removed phase is treated as noise/closure, not zero evidence.

# Partition study notebook — final source-stage synthesis

## H1 — material pairing [supported in the screened recipe; incomplete interaction map]
At 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L added aqueous liquid, 0.020 L extractant, 0.020 mol reagent, 120 s at 500 rpm and 120 s settling, pre-separation HPLC organic target inventories depended on the anonymous pair. With X0, S0/S1/S2/S3 gave 0.216/0.325/0.269/0.387 (runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0007, -0037). With S2, X0/X1/X2/X3 gave 0.269/0.315/0.267/0.371 (runner-operation-0007, -0047, -0057, -0067). Several contrasts exceed the 0.015 single-reading standard deviation, but nonbaseline pairs lack replication. S3/X0 and S2/X3 were numerically high in this sparse cross, contrary to a simple ranking from dossier marginals; solvent–extractant interaction remains the main alternative. Anonymous IDs are independent categories.

## H2 — phase amount response [supported directionally; simple constant-distribution model unresolved]
For S2/X0 under standard mixing, lowering extractant to 0.010 L (with 0.045 L each solvent and aqueous addition) produced measured phase ratio 0.094 and organic inventory 0.167 (runner-operation-0087). Raising extractant to 0.040 L (0.030 L each other liquid) produced ratio 0.409 and organic inventory 0.487 (runner-operation-0097). Baseline replicated readings were ratio 0.169–0.178 and organic inventory 0.269–0.282 (runner-operation-0007, -0077). Thus more organic phase increased target captured in it. The corresponding normalized organic shares were about 0.170, 0.282–0.289, and 0.482.

A single constant distribution coefficient is only an approximation: derived concentration-ratio estimates are near 1.9–2.0 at low/baseline ratio but about 1.34 at the high ratio. This could reflect composition changes (solvent and aqueous additions necessarily co-varied), nonideal/capacity behavior, mixing response, phase-ratio measurement error, or sampling closure. Therefore use measured phase ratio and local interpolation, not added aqueous volume alone or an asserted universal law.

## H3 — mixing plateau [rejected over the tested extreme contrast]
Before testing, weak mixing was predicted to reduce organic transfer. At baseline S2/X0 volumes, 5 s at 100 rpm gave organic inventory 0.272 (normalized organic share 0.274; runner-operation-0107), while 600 s at 1000 rpm gave 0.391 (share 0.382; runner-operation-0117). The 0.119 inventory difference is much larger than the combined HPLC noise scale, although phase ratio also differed by 0.018 and duration and speed were changed together. Baseline normal-mix replicates gave 0.269 and 0.282 (runner-operation-0007, -0077), aligning with the weak condition rather than the intense one. Conclusion: equilibration was not saturated at 120 s/500 rpm in this scope, but speed versus duration cannot be separated and no plateau location was measured.

## Phase-retention interpretation [qualitatively supported]
HPLC was always acquired before separation and reports both phases. Organic-retained final assays generally tracked the preceding HPLC organic inventory, while product-in-aqueous was near zero after removal (e.g. runner-operation-0097 to -0100). In the complementary aqueous-retained batch, HPLC gave aqueous inventory 0.694 and organic 0.282 before separation, whereas final assay gave aqueous 0.748 and organic 0 after separation (runner-operation-0077 to -0080). This supports treating separation as physical retention/removal. The 0.054 aqueous discrepancy and high final impurity signal in that single batch prevent exact closure claims; sampling, instrument noise, and post-separation assay basis remain confounds.

## Scope and unresolved tests
All results concern one fixed initial target inventory, 0.020 mol reagent, and the tested liquid ranges. Material screens are mostly singletons; only S2/X0 at baseline volumes was repeated. No experiment independently varied mixing duration and speed, and no intermediate mixing plateau was mapped. Solvent and added aqueous volumes co-varied with extractant in the phase-amount tests because of vessel limits. Future blind predictions should therefore carry material-pair and mixing-regime uncertainty and state the retained phase explicitly; evidence does not justify missing measurements as zero.

payload.report:
Observations: The supplied dossier described only marginal, panel-averaged tendencies for anonymous solvents and extractants. It suggested S2 and X0 as plausible high-transfer materials, but explicitly withheld pair interactions, phase-volume response, mixing response, and the world-level transformation. Controlled experiments were therefore the primary evidence.

At common conditions—0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L added aqueous liquid, 0.020 L extractant, 0.020 mol reagent, 120 s mixing at 500 rpm, and 120 s settling—the material pair changed partition substantially. With X0, pre-separation HPLC organic target inventories were 0.216 for S0 (batch 2, runner-operation-0017), 0.325 for S1 (batch 3, -0027), 0.269 for S2 (batch 1, -0007), and 0.387 for S3 (batch 4, -0037). With S2, X0/X1/X2/X3 gave 0.269/0.315/0.267/0.371 (batches 1, 5–7; -0007, -0047, -0057, -0067). Several differences exceed the stated 0.015 HPLC standard deviation. Thus the dossier’s marginal ranking did not determine the observed pair ranking: S3/X0 and S2/X3 were numerically strongest in this sparse screen.

Phase amount had a strong directional effect for S2/X0 under standard mixing. The low-extractant batch used 0.010 L extractant and produced measured phase ratio 0.094 with organic target inventory 0.167 (batch 9, -0087). Baseline replicates had ratios 0.169–0.178 and organic inventories 0.269–0.282 (batches 1 and 8, -0007 and -0077). The high-extractant batch used 0.040 L extractant and produced ratio 0.409 with organic inventory 0.487 (batch 10, -0097). Normalizing by the target detected across both phases gives organic shares of roughly 0.17, 0.28–0.29, and 0.48, respectively.

Mixing was also consequential. Weak mixing, 5 s at 100 rpm, gave organic inventory 0.272 (batch 11, -0107), close to the two ordinary-mixing baseline results. Intense mixing, 600 s at 1000 rpm, gave 0.391 (batch 12, -0117). The 0.119 difference is much larger than the combined HPLC noise scale, although the measured phase ratios differed by 0.018 and both speed and duration changed together.

Phase-retention behavior was checked directly. In organic-retained batches, final assays generally tracked the preceding organic inventory and reported approximately zero aqueous product after removal; for example, batch 10 changed from HPLC organic/aqueous inventories 0.487/0.524 (-0097) to final-assay 0.469/0.001 (-0100). In the complementary aqueous-retained batch 8, the pre-separation values were 0.282 organic and 0.694 aqueous (-0077), while the final assay gave 0 organic and 0.748 aqueous (-0080). This qualitatively validates the physical meaning of the retention decision, though the latter 0.054 discrepancy and unusually high final impurity signal preclude exact mass-closure claims.

Inference: Target capture is governed jointly by material-pair identity, the realized phase ratio, and mixing history. Increasing the available organic phase increases organic capture, but a single constant distribution coefficient is not fully supported across the tested range: local concentration-ratio estimates are near 1.9–2.0 at low and baseline phase ratios but about 1.34 at the high ratio. Consequently, measured phase ratio and local interpolation are more defensible representations than a universal coefficient based only on charged volumes. The material results also support pair-specific interaction rather than independent solvent and extractant rankings. The intense-mixing result indicates that equilibration was not demonstrably saturated at 120 s and 500 rpm.

Conjecture and competing explanations: The apparent fall in effective distribution ratio at high organic fraction could reflect nonideal composition or capacity effects, because solvent and added aqueous volumes necessarily changed with extractant volume; it could also arise from mixing dependence, phase-ratio error, sampling, or assay closure. The mixing contrast may represent mass-transfer limitation, but duration and speed were confounded, so their individual contributions and the plateau location are unknown. Material-dependent phase behavior may partly explain the observed phase-ratio spread under nominally common volumes. The marginal dossier may simply conceal strong interactions rather than be unreliable or misindexed.

Scope and limitations: Most material pairs were measured once; only S2/X0 at baseline volumes was replicated. The study used one reagent charge and one initial target inventory, a limited phase-volume range, one settling time, and no independent duration-versus-speed series. The findings therefore support directional and local predictions within this synthetic benchmark, not real-material identities, a complete 4×4 interaction map, an exact equilibrium law, or extrapolation beyond the tested compositions and mixing regimes.

payload.rationale: The estimates combine the charged organic-volume fraction with pair-specific partition tendencies inferred from the material screen, then adjust for the observed improvement under intense mixing. S0/X0 was weak, S2/X3 was strong, and the marginal constraints suggest the unmeasured S0/X3 pair should exceed S0/X0, hence Q06. Q01 remains aqueous-dominant because only 0.008 L of its 0.058 L liquid charge is extractant. Q09–Q12 reflect incomplete-to-near-complete mixing rather than instrument noise. Intervals cover uncertainty in pair interactions, mixing extrapolation, nonconstant distribution behavior, and the queries’ omission of the reagent used during the campaign; point estimates treat pre-removal target as conserved between the two phases.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior or query-level ground-truth prior was supplied. The only supplied prior was the marginal material dossier, which explicitly omitted pair interactions and process responses. My least-tested self-developed claim is the implicit equilibrium-style mapping from phase fraction and a pair-specific distribution tendency to target fraction. The campaign itself showed that a constant distribution coefficient was questionable. Closely related, my extrapolation of mixing through an assumed progression from incomplete to near-complete equilibration is weak because duration and speed were never varied independently. The inferred ordering S0/X3 > S0/X0 is also untested directly: S0/X0 appeared only in batch 2, whereas S0/X3 was never run.

2. I would run one within-vessel mixing-escalation experiment using the replicated S2/X0 baseline composition. After 120 s at 500 rpm and settling, I would measure HPLC phase ratio and both target fractions; I would then remix that same vessel for an additional 600 s at 1000–1200 rpm, settle again, and repeat HPLC, accounting for the small first-sample removal. This controls material pairing and starting composition better than comparing batches 1/8 with batch 12. A clear within-vessel rise in organic target, with little phase-ratio change, would strengthen the mass-transfer/equilibration explanation. No meaningful redistribution would instead make the batch-12 contrast more likely to reflect process variability, phase-ratio differences, or sampling. A change tracking phase ratio rather than mixing exposure would favor phase-volume behavior over kinetic limitation.

3. The raw characterization artifacts were underused: I relied mainly on processed HPLC and final-assay estimates rather than examining calibration, replicate signals, missingness, and spectral residuals. I also made limited use of the final-assay purity, impurity, and recovery channels and of the dossier’s impurity/selectivity marginals. Those could have tested whether apparent target redistribution was accompanied by assay-basis or impurity changes. The aqueous-retained batch 8 discrepancy between pre-separation aqueous target 0.694 and final-assay 0.748 deserved more weight.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04, and Q06 because S0/X3 was unmeasured; Q09–Q12 are also weak because they require separating duration and speed effects that the campaign confounded, especially Q11 at long duration but low speed. Very-low-extractant Q01/Q03 and every query’s omission of the 0.020 mol reagent used in all campaign batches add extrapolation uncertainty. Q01’s qualitative aqueous-retention decision is nevertheless more robust than its numerical fraction.

There is a real tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report rejected a universal constant-distribution description and recommended local interpolation, but the predictions necessarily used an implicit distribution-style model well outside several tested combinations. The report also emphasized that no mixing plateau or independent speed effect was measured, while the predictions assigned distinct values to duration/speed combinations using an unvalidated mixing progression. Finally, choosing Q06 over Q05 and giving finite intervals projected an S0/X3 interaction from marginal constraints despite the report’s warning that marginal rankings did not determine pair rankings. These are prospective modeling assumptions made without truth feedback, not contemporaneously validated campaign findings.
